claim: The phage-inducible chromosomal island-like element (PLE) integrates into the chromosome of Vibrio cholerae.
source: The phage-inducible chromosomal island-like element (PLE) is a mobile element that integrates into the chromosome of Vibrio cholerae and parasitizes the bacteriophage ICP1 to move between cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of PLE's behavior.

claim: PLE parasitizes the bacteriophage ICP1 to move between cells.
source: The phage-inducible chromosomal island-like element (PLE) is a mobile element that integrates into the chromosome of Vibrio cholerae and parasitizes the bacteriophage ICP1 to move between cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing PLE's mechanism of mobility.

claim: PLE parasitism abolishes the production of ICP1 progeny.
source: This parasitism by PLE is such that it abolishes the production of ICP1 progeny and provides a defensive boon to the host cell population.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an outcome of PLE parasitism.

claim: PLE provides a defensive boon to the host cell population.
source: This parasitism by PLE is such that it abolishes the production of ICP1 progeny and provides a defensive boon to the host cell population.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a consequence of PLE activity.

claim: ICP1 has acquired an adaptive CRISPR-Cas system that targets the PLE genome during infection.
source: In response to the severe parasitism imposed by PLE, ICP1 has acquired an adaptive CRISPR-Cas system that targets the PLE genome during infection.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as ICP1's counter-defense mechanism.

claim: ICP1 isolates that naturally lack CRISPR-Cas are still able to overcome certain PLE variants.
source: However, ICP1 isolates that naturally lack CRISPR-Cas are still able to overcome certain PLE variants, and the mechanism of this immunity against PLE has thus far remained unknown.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an observation that motivated the study.

claim: ICP1 isolates that lack CRISPR-Cas encode an endonuclease in the same locus.
source: Here, we show that ICP1 isolates that lack CRISPR-Cas encode an endonuclease in the same locus, and that the endonuclease provides ICP1 with immunity to a subset of PLEs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The endonuclease provides ICP1 with immunity to a subset of PLEs.
source: Here, we show that ICP1 isolates that lack CRISPR-Cas encode an endonuclease in the same locus, and that the endonuclease provides ICP1 with immunity to a subset of PLEs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The endonuclease is of chimeric origin, incorporating a DNA-binding domain that is highly similar to some PLE replication origin-binding proteins.
source: Further analysis shows that this endonuclease is of chimeric origin, incorporating a DNA-binding domain that is highly similar to some PLE replication origin-binding proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The similarity of the endonuclease DNA-binding domain to PLE origin-binding proteins allows the endonuclease to bind and cleave PLE origins of replication.
source: This similarity allows the endonuclease to bind and cleave PLE origins of replication.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion stated in the abstract based on experimental findings.

claim: The endonuclease appears to exert considerable selective pressure on PLEs.
source: The endonuclease appears to exert considerable selective pressure on PLEs and may drive PLE replication module swapping and origin restructuring as mechanisms of escape.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on evolutionary analysis.

claim: The endonuclease may drive PLE replication module swapping and origin restructuring as mechanisms of escape.
source: The endonuclease appears to exert considerable selective pressure on PLEs and may drive PLE replication module swapping and origin restructuring as mechanisms of escape.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the abstract.

claim: New genome defense systems can arise through domain shuffling.
source: This work demonstrates that new genome defense systems can arise through domain shuffling and provides a greater understanding of the evolutionary forces driving genome modularity and temporal succession in mobile elements.
evidence: This is a general conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: Mobile genetic elements are key mediators of evolution.
source: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs), genetic units capable of spreading within and between genomes, are key mediators of evolution.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Homing endonucleases are single-gene MGEs that occur in diploid loci and cleave cognate alleles so that their coding sequences can serve as templates for recombinational repair.
source: At one end of the spectrum are homing endonucleases (HEGs). These single-gene MGEs occur in diploid loci and cleave cognate alleles so that their coding sequences can serve as templates for recombinational repair (Stoddard, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Integrative viruses can encode their own replication genes as well as structural components for their own dispersal.
source: At another extreme, integrative viruses are complex MGEs that can encode their own replication genes as well as structural components for their own dispersal (Krupovic et al., 2019), and even cargo genes dedicated to boosting the fitness of their cellular hosts (Harrison and Brockhurst, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Short generation times and low barriers to horizontal gene transfer make bacteria ideal organisms for studying how MGEs shape the evolution of their hosts.
source: In contrast, short generation times and low barriers to horizontal gene transfer make bacteria ideal organisms for studying how MGEs shape the evolution of their hosts.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale in the introduction.

claim: MGEs frequently encode defense modules to prevent infection by viruses or other nonvirus MGEs.
source: MGEs frequently encode defense modules to prevent infection by viruses or other nonvirus MGEs (Koonin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Defense modules include toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems, restriction modification (RM) systems, CRISPR-Cas, and numerous other systems recently described.
source: Such modules include toxin-antitoxin (TA) systems, restriction modification (RM) systems, CRISPR-Cas, and numerous other systems recently described (Doron et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2020; Koonin and Makarova, 2019; Marraffini, 2015; Millman et al., 2020; Mruk and Kobayashi, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Defense systems serve the selfish needs of the MGEs that encode them.
source: Beyond their antiviral and anti-MGE functions, defense systems also serve the selfish needs of the MGEs that encode them, and the constituents of defense modules can be recruited to benefit viruses and nonvirus MGEs by serving counter-defense functions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Viruses may encode antitoxin or DNA modification genes as a means of escaping TA and RM systems endogenous to their hosts.
source: Viruses may encode antitoxin or DNA modification genes as a means of escaping TA and RM systems endogenous to their hosts (Loenen and Raleigh, 2014; Otsuka and Yonesaki, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Many phages use nucleases to degrade the host genome, preventing further expression of host defenses.
source: While many defense modules eliminate invading viruses and MGEs through nucleolytic attack, many phages use nucleases to degrade the host genome, preventing further expression of host defenses (McKitterick et al., 2019a; Panayotatos and Fontaine, 1985; Parson and Snustad, 1975; Souther et al., 1972; Warner et al., 1975).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Upon infection by ICP1, PLE excises from the host chromosome.
source: Upon infection by ICP1, PLE excises from the host chromosome, replicates to high copy (O'Hara et al., 2017), and is assembled into transducing particles to spread the PLE genome to new cells (Netter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: PLE replicates to high copy upon ICP1 infection.
source: Upon infection by ICP1, PLE excises from the host chromosome, replicates to high copy (O'Hara et al., 2017), and is assembled into transducing particles to spread the PLE genome to new cells (Netter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: PLE is assembled into transducing particles to spread the PLE genome to new cells.
source: Upon infection by ICP1, PLE excises from the host chromosome, replicates to high copy (O'Hara et al., 2017), and is assembled into transducing particles to spread the PLE genome to new cells (Netter et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: PLE excision and DNA replication both require ICP1-encoded gene products.
source: PLE excision and DNA replication both require ICP1-encoded gene products (Barth et al., 2020b; McKitterick et al., 2019a; McKitterick and Seed, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: PLE is packaged into remodeled ICP1 virions for mobilization.
source: Similarly, multiple lines of evidence including shared host cell receptors (O'Hara et al., 2017), PLE genome analysis, and electron microscopy (Netter et al., 2021) strongly suggest that PLE is packaged into remodeled ICP1 virions for mobilization.
evidence: This is stated as a strongly supported inference with citations.

claim: No ICP1 virions are produced when PLE activity is unimpeded.
source: While infected PLE(+) cells still die, no ICP1 virions are produced when PLE activity is unimpeded (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: PLE prevents further spread of ICP1 and protects the host cell population.
source: Thus, PLE prevents further spread of ICP1 and protects the host cell population.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on previous findings.

claim: PLE acts as both a selfish parasite of ICP1 and an effective abortive infection defense system for V. cholerae.
source: In this way, PLE acts as both a selfish parasite of ICP1 and an effective abortive infection defense system for V. cholerae.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of PLE's dual role.

claim: Many ICP1 isolates encode a CRISPR-Cas system that can destroy PLE within the infected cell and restore ICP1 reproduction.
source: Many ICP1 isolates encode a CRISPR-Cas system that can destroy PLE within the infected cell and restore ICP1 reproduction (Seed et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: CRISPR-Cas systems are typically adaptive immune systems that provide immunological memory against specific nucleic acid sequences.
source: CRISPR-Cas systems are typically adaptive immune systems that provide immunological memory against specific nucleic acid sequences (Barrangou et al., 2007; Marraffini, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The memory function of CRISPR-Cas is achieved through the integration of 'spacers,' short DNA sequences derived from viruses or MGEs.
source: The memory function of CRISPR-Cas is achieved through the integration of 'spacers,' short DNA sequences derived from viruses or MGEs, that are integrated into an array of spacer repeats.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CRISPR-Cas mechanism.

claim: Almost all spacers associated with ICP1's CRISPR-Cas system are PLE derived.
source: Reflecting the primary role of ICP1's CRISPR-Cas as an anti-PLE system, almost all spacers associated with the system are PLE derived (Seed et al., 2013; McKitterick et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations.

claim: The ICP1 CRISPR-Cas system can acquire new immunological memory.
source: Like cellular CRISPR-Cas systems, the ICP1 system can acquire new immunological memory, reflecting that PLE is not a single static genome but that a number of PLE variants exist.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about ICP1's CRISPR-Cas system.

claim: Five PLE variants, numbered 1–5, have been described to date.
source: To date, five PLE variants, numbered 1–5, have been described, occurring in about ~15% of sequenced epidemic V. cholerae genomes.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of known PLE diversity.

claim: PLE variants occur in about ~15% of sequenced epidemic V. cholerae genomes.
source: To date, five PLE variants, numbered 1–5, have been described, occurring in about ~15% of sequenced epidemic V. cholerae genomes.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative observation.

claim: There is a pattern of temporal succession where one PLE will dominate in sequenced genomes for a time before being supplanted by another PLE.
source: There is a pattern of temporal succession, where one PLE will dominate in sequenced genomes for a time before being supplanted by another PLE (O'Hara et al., 2017), but the reemergence of old PLE sequence in new PLE variants suggests that unsampled reservoirs exist in nature.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation.

claim: The reemergence of old PLE sequence in new PLE variants suggests that unsampled reservoirs exist in nature.
source: There is a pattern of temporal succession, where one PLE will dominate in sequenced genomes for a time before being supplanted by another PLE (O'Hara et al., 2017), but the reemergence of old PLE sequence in new PLE variants suggests that unsampled reservoirs exist in nature.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on observations.

claim: Not all ICP1 isolates encode CRISPR-Cas.
source: Like PLEs, there is also diversity among ICP1 genomes. Not all ICP1 isolates encode CRISPR-Cas, but this does not mean that they are defenseless against PLEs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about ICP1 diversity.

claim: An ICP1 variant that naturally lacked CRISPR-Cas was able to reproduce on PLE5, PLE4, and PLE1.
source: Previous work found that an ICP1 variant that naturally lacked CRISPR-Cas was able to reproduce on the two oldest PLE variants, PLE5 and PLE4, as well as the most recent variant PLE1 (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with a citation.

claim: There appears to be some temporal succession in the presence or absence of ICP1's CRISPR-Cas system.
source: Much like PLE variants, there appears to be some temporal succession in the presence or absence of ICP1's CRISPR-Cas system.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about ICP1 evolution.

claim: A minority of ICP1 isolates collected between 2001 and 2011 possessed CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: A minority of ICP1 isolates collected between 2001 and 2011 possessed CRISPR-Cas systems (Angermeyer et al., 2018), while CRISPR-Cas encoding ICP1 predominated between 2011 and 2017 (McKitterick et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation.

claim: CRISPR-Cas encoding ICP1 predominated between 2011 and 2017.
source: A minority of ICP1 isolates collected between 2001 and 2011 possessed CRISPR-Cas systems (Angermeyer et al., 2018), while CRISPR-Cas encoding ICP1 predominated between 2011 and 2017 (McKitterick et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation.

claim: In isolates without CRISPR-Cas, the locus is replaced with a single open reading frame, designated gp88.
source: In isolates without CRISPR-Cas, the locus is replaced with a single open reading frame, designated gp88 for its location in ICP12001, the original sequenced ICP1 isolate (Seed et al., 2011; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Gp88 encodes a T5orf172 domain containing protein.
source: Further analysis of gp88 revealed that it encodes a T5orf172 domain (pfam10544) containing protein.
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence analysis.

claim: The T5orf172 domain is a member of the GIY-YIG endonuclease domain superfamily.
source: This domain is a member of the GIY-YIG endonuclease domain superfamily, suggesting that Gp88 may be a nuclease.
evidence: This is stated as a result of domain analysis.

claim: Unlike most identified GIY-YIG nucleases, Gp88 lacks a conserved histidine or tyrosine in the first alpha helix of the GIY-YIG domain.
source: Unlike most identified GIY-YIG nucleases, Gp88 lacks a conserved histidine or tyrosine in the first alpha helix of the GIY-YIG domain.
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Gp88 retains conservation of the catalytic arginine and glutamate.
source: However, Gp88 retains conservation of the catalytic arginine and glutamate.
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The PLE (-) V. cholerae strain was susceptible to all ICP1 variants.
source: As expected, the PLE (-) V. cholerae strain was susceptible to all ICP1 variants, and the ICP12006 ∆CRISPR variant was restricted by all PLEs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The ICP12006 ∆CRISPR variant was restricted by all PLEs.
source: As expected, the PLE (-) V. cholerae strain was susceptible to all ICP1 variants, and the ICP12006 ∆CRISPR variant was restricted by all PLEs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: CRISPR(+) ICP12006 was able to propagate on all strains except the one containing PLE3.
source: CRISPR(+) ICP12006 was able to propagate on all strains except the one containing PLE3 as ICP12006 does not have a matching spacer against PLE3.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: ICP12006 does not have a matching spacer against PLE3.
source: CRISPR(+) ICP12006 was able to propagate on all strains except the one containing PLE3 as ICP12006 does not have a matching spacer against PLE3.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the experimental result.

claim: ICP12001 was able to propagate on PLEs 1, 4, and 5.
source: ICP12001 was able to propagate on PLEs 1, 4, and 5 (Figure 2A), but it was restricted on PLEs 2 and 3.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: ICP12001 was restricted on PLEs 2 and 3.
source: ICP12001 was able to propagate on PLEs 1, 4, and 5 (Figure 2A), but it was restricted on PLEs 2 and 3.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: The ∆gp88 and gp88* mutants were unable to propagate on V. cholerae with PLEs 1, 4, or 5.
source: Unlike the wild-type (WT) variant, the ∆gp88 and gp88* mutants were unable to propagate on V. cholerae with PLEs 1, 4, or 5 (Figure 2A), indicating that catalytically active gp88 is necessary for overcoming these PLEs in phages naturally lacking CRISPR-Cas.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Catalytically active gp88 is necessary for overcoming PLEs 1, 4, and 5 in phages naturally lacking CRISPR-Cas.
source: Unlike the wild-type (WT) variant, the ∆gp88 and gp88* mutants were unable to propagate on V. cholerae with PLEs 1, 4, or 5 (Figure 2A), indicating that catalytically active gp88 is necessary for overcoming these PLEs in phages naturally lacking CRISPR-Cas.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from experimental results.

claim: The gp88 mutants retained sensitivity to restriction by PLEs 2 and 3.
source: Unsurprisingly, the gp88 mutants retained sensitivity to restriction by PLEs 2 and 3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: PLE1 is unable to replicate in the presence of Gp88 encoding ICP1.
source: We observed that PLE1 is unable to replicate in the presence of Gp88 encoding ICP1, and replication is restored during infection with the Gp88 knockout or catalytically inactive mutant phages (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: PLE1 replication is restored during infection with the Gp88 knockout or catalytically inactive mutant phages.
source: We observed that PLE1 is unable to replicate in the presence of Gp88 encoding ICP1, and replication is restored during infection with the Gp88 knockout or catalytically inactive mutant phages (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The PLE1 copy decreases following infection by Gp88 encoding phage.
source: Consistent with endonucleolytic activity, the PLE1 copy decreases following infection by Gp88 encoding phage.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Multiple PLE matched spacers are required for CRISPR-Cas to completely abolish PLE replication during infection.
source: This is notable given that previous work has shown that multiple PLE matched spacers are required for CRISPR-Cas to completely abolish PLE replication during infection (McKitterick et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated as previous knowledge with a citation.

claim: PLE2 replication is unaffected by the presence or absence of Gp88.
source: PLE2 replication is unaffected by the presence or absence of Gp88, consistent with Gp88 not providing ICP1 with immunity against PLE2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Only two stretches of sequence were uniquely present or uniquely absent in PLEs 2 and 3: the repA gene and the intergenic region containing the PLE origin of replication.
source: Strikingly, only two stretches of sequence met these criteria, and both had been previously implicated in PLE replication (Barth et al., 2020b). The repA gene encoding the replication initiation factor, and the intergenic region containing the PLE origin of replication (ori) to which RepA binds covaried, with the PLE1, 4, and 5 sequences clustering together as one group, and the PLE2 and 3 sequences clustering as another (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparative genomic analysis with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The repA gene and the origin of replication covaried, with PLE1, 4, and 5 sequences clustering together as one group, and PLE2 and 3 sequences clustering as another.
source: The repA gene encoding the replication initiation factor, and the intergenic region containing the PLE origin of replication (ori) to which RepA binds covaried, with the PLE1, 4, and 5 sequences clustering together as one group, and the PLE2 and 3 sequences clustering as another (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparative genomic analysis with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: It was the DNA-binding RepA_N domain of RepA that covaried with the origin, while the C-terminal domain was conserved across all PLEs.
source: More specifically, it was the DNA-binding RepA_N domain of RepA that covaried with the origin, while the C-terminal domain, hypothesized to facilitate replisome recruitment (Barth et al., 2020b), was conserved across all PLEs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence analysis with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Ectopic expression of RepA was sufficient to drive replication of a synthetic 'midiPLE' construct during ICP1 infection.
source: Previously, we found that during ICP1 infection, ectopic expression of RepA was sufficient to drive replication of a synthetic 'midiPLE' construct.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding.

claim: MidiPLE replication did not occur without RepA.
source: Additionally, midiPLE replication did not occur without RepA, and the PLE integrase was shown to be dispensable for PLE replication (Barth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with a citation.

claim: The PLE integrase was shown to be dispensable for PLE replication.
source: Additionally, midiPLE replication did not occur without RepA, and the PLE integrase was shown to be dispensable for PLE replication (Barth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with a citation.

claim: The minimal components of the PLE replicon are the replication origin and RepA.
source: These data suggest that the minimal components of the PLE replicon are the replication origin and RepA, the two components that covaried across PLEs.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from previous data.

claim: Alignment of the conserved 3′ ends of PLE repA genes suggests that RepA specificity swapping has occurred multiple times.
source: Alignment of the conserved 3′ ends of PLE repA genes suggests that RepA specificity swapping has occurred multiple times (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from sequence alignment with reference to figures.

claim: The PLE1 RepA_N domain clusters with the PLE4 and PLE5 variants, but the PLE1 C-terminal sequence is more similar to PLE2 than PLE5.
source: Despite the PLE1 RepA_N domain clustering with the PLE4 and PLE5 variants, the PLE1 C-terminal sequence is more similar to PLE2 (98.88% identical over the last 178 bp) than PLE5 (93.25% identical over the last 178 bp).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence comparison.

claim: PLE5 and PLE3 are 99.44% identical over the C-terminal region.
source: PLE5 and PLE3 are 99.44% identical over the same region, while the PLE4 C-terminal region is the most diverged from other PLEs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence comparison with reference to a figure.

claim: PLE replisome module swapping occurred at least twice.
source: This cross-clustering of repA ends would only be expected to occur after multiple gene recombination events, suggesting that PLE replisome module swapping occurred at least twice, and may be an important part of PLE evolution.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from sequence analysis.

claim: Deletion of the putative PLE2 origin abolished replication following infection by ICP12006 ∆CRISPR.
source: We first tested whether the putative PLE2 origin and repA gene were necessary for PLE2 replication and found that deletion of either component abolished replication following infection by ICP12006 ∆CRISPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), as was previously observed for PLE1 (Barth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to a figure.

claim: Deletion of the PLE2 repA gene abolished replication following infection by ICP12006 ∆CRISPR.
source: We first tested whether the putative PLE2 origin and repA gene were necessary for PLE2 replication and found that deletion of either component abolished replication following infection by ICP12006 ∆CRISPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), as was previously observed for PLE1 (Barth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to a figure.

claim: PLE replication only occurred when cognate origins and repA alleles co-occurred.
source: As expected, PLE replication only occurred when cognate origins and repA alleles co-occurred, revealing that the two components of the PLE replicon function together as a module, irrespective of which PLE backbone they are encoded in.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result from origin-swapping experiments.

claim: Gp88's N-terminal domain is 42% identical and 61% sequence similar across 93% of PLE1's RepA_N domain.
source: Remarkably, Gp88's own N-terminal domain is 42% identical and 61% sequence similar across 93% of PLE1's RepA_N domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence comparison with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Gp88's T5orf172 domain is similar to those of several putative HEGs within the ICP1 genome.
source: This was surprising as Gp88's T5orf172 domain is similar to those of several putative HEGs within the ICP1 genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence comparison with reference to a figure.

claim: gp88 may have arisen as a chimeric hybrid of PLE and ICP1 coding sequences.
source: The high similarity of Gp88's N-terminal portion to some PLE-encoded RepA alleles and the C-terminal portions similarity to putative HEGs suggest that gp88 may have arisen as a chimeric hybrid of PLE and ICP1 coding sequences.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from sequence analysis.

claim: Deletion of the entire conserved stretch of sequence that contained the origin of replication in PLEs 1, 4, and 5 allowed these mutants to regain restrictive activity against Gp88 encoding phage.
source: We tested this by deleting the entire conserved stretch of sequence that contained the origin of replication in PLEs 1, 4, and 5. In support of our hypothesis, these mutants regained restrictive activity against Gp88 encoding phage (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The PLE2 ∆ori strain retained the ability to restrict all isolates of ICP12001.
source: The PLE2 ∆ori strain retained the ability to restrict all isolates of ICP12001 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The PLE2 strain bearing the PLE1 origin sequence was no longer restrictive to ICP12001, but still restricted variants that lacked Gp88 activity.
source: In contrast, the PLE2 strain bearing the PLE1 origin sequence was no longer restrictive to ICP12001, but still restricted variants that lacked Gp88 activity (Figure 4C), confirming that the presence of the replication origin sequence mediated sensitivity to Gp88.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Purified Gp88 protein cut PCR products amplified from the region containing the origin of replication from PLEs 1, 4, and 5, but did not cut those of PLEs 2 and 3.
source: Consistent with the host range of ICP1 encoding Gp88, we found that the purified Gp88 protein cut PCR products amplified from the region containing the origin of replication from PLEs 1, 4, and 5, but did not cut those of PLEs 2 and 3 (Figure 4D), confirming that Gp88 disrupts PLE through nuclease activity.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The E180A Gp88* mutant did not cleave PCR products amplified from PLEs 1, 4, and 5.
source: Supporting this interpretation, the E180A Gp88* mutant that was inactive against PLEs 1, 4, and 5 in vivo, and predicted to be catalytically inert, did not cleave PCR products amplified from PLEs 1, 4, and 5 (Figure 4E), further linking the in vivo activity of Gp88 to its capacity to cleave in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: PLE1 RepA was found to bind specifically to a set of iterons, a series of three ~30 bp semi-palindromic repeats in the PLE1 origin of replication.
source: Previously, PLE1 RepA was found to bind specifically to a set of iterons, a series of three ~30 bp semi-palindromic repeats in the PLE1 origin of replication (Barth et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with a citation.

claim: Odn requires the iteron sequence for cleavage.
source: In support of our model, we found that Odn does require the iteron sequence for cleavage (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: ICP12001 infection was restricted by a PLE1 strain harboring the iteron deletion.
source: Consistent with iterons being necessary for Odn-mediated in vitro cleavage of the PLE origin, ICP12001 infection was restricted by a PLE1 strain harboring the same iteron deletion (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Odn has DNA-binding specificity that mimics that of the replication initiation factor of some PLEs.
source: Together, these results strongly support that Odn has DNA-binding specificity that mimics that of the replication initiation factor of some PLEs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from experimental results.

claim: A single instance of diversity in PLE1 was found within a lineage of V. cholerae isolated from Pakistan.
source: However, we found a single instance of diversity in PLE1 within a lineage of V. cholerae isolated from Pakistan. This lineage was represented in five sequenced strains (biosample accession numbers SAMN08979118, SAMN08979175, SAMN08979185, SAMN08979188, and SAMN08979253).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from genomic data.

claim: In five V. cholerae strains from Pakistan, variation in a 67 bp stretch covering the iterons results in several nucleotide changes.
source: In these five strains, we discovered variation in a 67 bp stretch covering the iterons that results in several nucleotide changes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence analysis.

claim: Within the first iteron, there is an A to T transversion, and starting at that transversion, the next 42 bp are duplicated and replace the sequence that is normally downstream.
source: Within the first iteron, there is an A to T transversion, and starting at that transversion, the next 42 bp are duplicated and replace the sequence that is normally downstream (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the sequence variation with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The PLE1Mut sequence was notably less susceptible to cleavage by Odn than the WT allele.
source: The PLE1Mut sequence was notably less susceptible to cleavage by Odn than the WT allele, but some cutting of the PLE1Mut probe at the highest concentration of Odn was apparent (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: The PLE1Mut origin of replication was able to drive replication to levels comparable to that of the WT origin.
source: The PLE1Mut origin of replication was able to drive replication to levels comparable to that of the WT origin, and robust replication was maintained even in the presence of Odn (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Robust replication of PLE1Mut was maintained even in the presence of Odn.
source: The PLE1Mut origin of replication was able to drive replication to levels comparable to that of the WT origin, and robust replication was maintained even in the presence of Odn (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: The PLE1Mut strain restricted production of WT ICP12001.
source: In agreement with our replication data, we also found that our PLE1Mut strain restricted production of WT ICP12001 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result with reference to Figure 6E.

claim: PLE can escape Odn activity through subtle restructuring of the iterons.
source: These data demonstrate that PLE can escape Odn activity through subtle restructuring of the iterons, in addition to more extensive replication module exchange (Figure 3A), and suggest that ICP1 counter-defenses like Odn may select for diversification of the PLE replication machinery.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from experimental results.

claim: ICP1 counter-defenses like Odn may select for diversification of the PLE replication machinery.
source: These data demonstrate that PLE can escape Odn activity through subtle restructuring of the iterons, in addition to more extensive replication module exchange (Figure 3A), and suggest that ICP1 counter-defenses like Odn may select for diversification of the PLE replication machinery.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from experimental results.

claim: Odn possess two domains: an endonuclease domain and a DNA-binding domain.
source: The anti-PLE effector Odn possess two domains, an endonuclease domain and a DNA-binding domain, which has sequence similarity to the DNA-binding domain of the RepA initiation factor from PLEs 1, 4, and 5.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: Odn cuts the origin of replication in PLEs 1, 4, and 5.
source: Mimicking RepA's specificity, Odn cuts the origin of replication in those PLEs.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: PLEs are able to escape Odn antagonism through mutation of their origin of replication.
source: PLEs are able to escape Odn antagonism through mutation of their origin of replication, and there is compelling evidence suggesting that PLEs have exchanged replicon modules for an alternative replication origin and initiation factor origin-binding domain on at least two separate occasions.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: PLEs have exchanged replicon modules for an alternative replication origin and initiation factor origin-binding domain on at least two separate occasions.
source: PLEs are able to escape Odn antagonism through mutation of their origin of replication, and there is compelling evidence suggesting that PLEs have exchanged replicon modules for an alternative replication origin and initiation factor origin-binding domain on at least two separate occasions.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from sequence analysis in the discussion.

claim: The oldest ICP1 strains encode Odn and the oldest PLE variants encode the sensitive origin of replication.
source: While sampling of ICP1 isolates and V. cholerae strains is far from complete, we do see the oldest ICP1 strains encode Odn and the oldest PLE variants encode the sensitive origin of replication.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the discussion.

claim: Odn may have selected for alternative replicon modules, leading to the decline of PLE4 and succession of PLE2 that occurred in the early 2000s.
source: It is possible that Odn selected for alternative replicon modules, leading to the decline of PLE4 and succession of PLE2 that occurred in the early 2000s (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation in the discussion.

claim: The succession of PLE2 may have caused selection for the presence of CRISPR-Cas, a decrease in prominence of Odn, and the reemergence of the sensitive replicon module in PLE1.
source: This may in turn have caused selection for the presence of CRISPR-Cas, a decrease in prominence of Odn, and the reemergence of the sensitive replicon module in PLE1 matching the trends of PLE and ICP1 occurrence observed thus far (McKitterick et al., 2019b; O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation in the discussion.

claim: This model of PLE and ICP1 succession is consistent with an antagonistic frequency-dependent selection (aFDS) mechanism of host-pathogen coevolution.
source: This model of PLE and ICP1 succession is consistent with an antagonistic frequency-dependent selection (aFDS) mechanism of host-pathogen coevolution where some level of genetic diversity is maintained among antagonistic genes and rare alleles are selected for, leading to oscillation of the dominant genotype (Papkou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the discussion with a citation.

claim: An obvious benefit of Odn is its small size; odn is less than 700 bp and more than 10 times smaller than ICP1's CRISPR-Cas system.
source: An obvious benefit of Odn is its small size; odn is less than 700 bp and more than 10 times smaller than ICP1's CRISPR-Cas system.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the discussion.

claim: Odn may provide more complete restriction of certain PLEs than CRISPR-Cas.
source: Additionally, Odn may provide more complete restriction of certain PLEs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: A single CRISPR spacer is sufficient to enable ICP1 plaque formation on PLE(+) cells.
source: While a single CRISPR spacer is sufficient to enable ICP1 plaque formation on PLE(+) cells, it was previously found that multiple spacers were needed to completely abolish PLE replication, and PLE transduction could still be detected from single-spacer ICP1 infections (McKitterick et al., 2019b; O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as previous knowledge with citations.

claim: Multiple spacers were needed to completely abolish PLE replication.
source: While a single CRISPR spacer is sufficient to enable ICP1 plaque formation on PLE(+) cells, it was previously found that multiple spacers were needed to completely abolish PLE replication, and PLE transduction could still be detected from single-spacer ICP1 infections (McKitterick et al., 2019b; O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as previous knowledge with citations.

claim: PLE transduction could still be detected from single-spacer ICP1 infections.
source: While a single CRISPR spacer is sufficient to enable ICP1 plaque formation on PLE(+) cells, it was previously found that multiple spacers were needed to completely abolish PLE replication, and PLE transduction could still be detected from single-spacer ICP1 infections (McKitterick et al., 2019b; O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as previous knowledge with citations.

claim: Different CRISPR spacers had different outcomes in terms of PLE transduction and ICP1 reproduction.
source: Additionally, different CRISPR spacers had different outcomes in terms of PLE transduction and ICP1 reproduction (McKitterick et al., 2019b), suggesting that where PLE is targeted may be important.
evidence: This is stated as previous knowledge with a citation.

claim: By destroying the origin of replication, Odn-mediated PLE degradation might not have to compete with PLE replication and could head off pathways for PLE escape through recombinational repair.
source: By destroying the origin of replication, Odn-mediated PLE degradation might not have to compete with PLE replication and could head off pathways for PLE escape through recombinational repair.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: No PLEs appear to encode anti-CRISPRs.
source: While no PLEs appear to encode anti-CRISPRs, numerous anti-CRISPRs have been found in Gammaproteobacteria (Pawluk et al., 2016), and co-occurrence of these genes with PLE could neutralize ICP1's CRISPR-Cas as an anti-PLE strategy.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the discussion.

claim: Numerous anti-CRISPRs have been found in Gammaproteobacteria.
source: While no PLEs appear to encode anti-CRISPRs, numerous anti-CRISPRs have been found in Gammaproteobacteria (Pawluk et al., 2016), and co-occurrence of these genes with PLE could neutralize ICP1's CRISPR-Cas as an anti-PLE strategy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Co-occurrence of anti-CRISPR genes with PLE could neutralize ICP1's CRISPR-Cas as an anti-PLE strategy.
source: While no PLEs appear to encode anti-CRISPRs, numerous anti-CRISPRs have been found in Gammaproteobacteria (Pawluk et al., 2016), and co-occurrence of these genes with PLE could neutralize ICP1's CRISPR-Cas as an anti-PLE strategy.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: Odn lacks the flexibility provided by CRISPR adaptation but provides more reliable interference against a subset of PLE variants.
source: Overall, it appears that Odn lacks the flexibility provided by CRISPR adaptation but provides more reliable interference against a subset of PLE variants.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: At least one other anti-PLE mechanism has evolved as some CRISPR(+) ICP1 isolates are able to plaque on PLE2 when CRISPR is deleted.
source: In addition to ICP1 and Odn, at least one other anti-PLE mechanism has evolved as some CRISPR(+) ICP1 isolates are able to plaque on PLE2 when CRISPR is deleted (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation.

claim: The anti-PLE2 mechanism may have helped select against PLE2, leading to the emergence of PLE1.
source: Whatever this anti-PLE mechanism may be, it may have helped select against PLE2, leading to the emergence of PLE1 as another possible example of an aFDS dynamic in the ICP1-PLE arms race.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: It seems unlikely that the anti-PLE2 mechanism is specific to the alternative replicon module as PLE3, which has a similar replicon to PLE2, maintains restriction of those particular ICP1 isolates.
source: It seems unlikely that this anti-PLE2 mechanism is specific to the alternative replicon module as PLE3, which has a similar replicon to PLE2, maintains restriction of those particular ICP1 isolates (O'Hara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an inference with a citation.

claim: The co-occurrence of a separate anti-PLE mechanism in the same phage as a CRISPR-Cas system suggests that CRISPR-Cas may have weak spots in terms of PLE inhibition.
source: In any case, the co-occurrence of a separate anti-PLE mechanism in the same phage as a CRISPR-Cas system further suggests that CRISPR-Cas may have weak spots in terms of PLE inhibition.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the discussion.

claim: The PLE1Mut variant is able to escape Odn activity despite the new iteron sequences being largely similar to those that exist in PLEs 1, 4, and 5.
source: It is somewhat surprising that the PLE1Mut variant is able to escape Odn activity, given that the new iteron sequences are largely similar to those that exist in PLEs 1, 4, and 5.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the discussion.

claim: The most notable differences in PLE1Mut are an extra T/A base between the inverted sub-repeats in both the second and third iterons, and a reduction of space between the second and third iterons.
source: The most notable differences are an extra T/A base between the inverted sub-repeats in both the second and third iterons, and a reduction of space between the second and third iterons (now 5 bp instead of 14 or 16 bp) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The changes in PLE1Mut appear more consistent with some sort of steric effect on catalysis from improper spacing rather than a loss of sequence recognition.
source: These changes appear more consistent with some sort of steric effect on catalysis from improper spacing rather than a loss of sequence recognition; however, the molecular details of Odn binding and catalysis remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the discussion.

claim: The T4-encoded GIY-YIG HEG I-TevI has two separate target specificities, one for DNA binding and one for cleavage, and cleavage is only efficient if the two recognition sites are properly spaced.
source: The T4-encoded GIY-YIG HEG I-TevI is known to have two separate target specificities, one for DNA binding and one for cleavage, and cleavage is only efficient if the two recognition sites are properly spaced (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: It is possible that Odn nucleolytic activity also has some sequence specificity, and closer spacing of the iterons is sufficient to block binding and cleavage by Odn.
source: It is possible that Odn nucleolytic activity also has some sequence specificity, and closer spacing of the iterons is sufficient to block binding and cleavage by Odn.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: For I-TevI, the sequence requirements for cleavage are somewhat loose, making cleavage sites harder to predict from sequence alone.
source: For I-TevI, the sequence requirements for cleavage are somewhat loose (Roy et al., 2016), making cleavage sites harder to predict from sequence alone.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: RepA is thought to bind as dimer.
source: RepA is thought to bind as dimer (Barth et al., 2020b), but at least some GIY-YIG endonucleases, including I-TevI, function as monomers (Van Roey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: At least some GIY-YIG endonucleases, including I-TevI, function as monomers.

claim: Odn is the first example of an anti-MGE gene where a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein has been 'captured' and fused to an endonuclease domain as a means of destroying the very genome that the sequence originated from.
source: While viral 'capture' of host genes by genetic parasites for the purpose of manipulating gene expression is well described in both phage and eukaryotic viruses (Alcami, 2003; Bryan et al., 2008; Zeng and Chisholm, 2012), to our knowledge Odn is the first example of an anti-MGE gene where a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein has been 'captured' and fused to an endonuclease domain as a means of destroying the very genome that the sequence originated from.
evidence: This is stated as a claim of novelty in the discussion.

claim: Horizontal gene transfer can serve as a shortcut to acquiring new sequence-specific antagonists during antagonistic coevolution.
source: This highlights how horizontal gene transfer can serve as a shortcut to acquiring new sequence-specific antagonists during antagonistic coevolution and provides a slower evolving parallel to adaptive immunity through spacer acquisition.
evidence: This is stated as a general conclusion in the discussion.

claim: Two examples of horizontal transfer between ICP1 and PLE relate to the same family of HEGs.
source: It is striking that two examples of horizontal transfer between ICP1 and PLE relate to the same family of HEGs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the discussion.

claim: Domain shuffling has been described for HEGs previously.
source: Domain shuffling has been described for HEGs previously (Landthaler and Shub, 2003) and is likely especially adaptive for HEGs, which are thought to amplify within host genomes by acquiring new sequence specificities (Gogarten and Hilario, 2006; Roy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: HEGs are thought to amplify within host genomes by acquiring new sequence specificities.
source: Domain shuffling has been described for HEGs previously (Landthaler and Shub, 2003) and is likely especially adaptive for HEGs, which are thought to amplify within host genomes by acquiring new sequence specificities (Gogarten and Hilario, 2006; Roy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The domain architecture of some phage-encoded HEGs has been likened to 'beads on a string': with independent functional domains connected by linker sequences.
source: The domain architecture of some phage-encoded HEGs has been likened to 'beads on a string': with independent functional domains connected by linker sequences (Van Roey and Derbyshire, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Proteins with 'beads on a string' architecture might be more amenable to domain shuffling.
source: It is conceivable that proteins with this architecture might be more amenable to domain shuffling, and given the selfish nature of HEGs, they may have adaptations to tolerate or promote this shuffling as a means of diversification and dispersal.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claim: A specific link between HEGs and MGE antagonism had not been established prior to characterization of Odn.
source: While HEG domestication has been much discussed (Coughlan et al., 2020; Stoddard, 2011) and the connection between genome antagonism and nucleases is well established in bacteria (Koonin et al., 2020), a specific link between HEGs and MGE antagonism had not been established prior to characterization of Odn.
evidence: This is stated as a claim of novelty in the discussion.

claim: It is not clear if Odn has any intrinsic homing activity.
source: It is not clear if Odn has any intrinsic homing activity, but Odn may be able to cleave and replace CRISPR-Cas loci that have acquired spacers matching the Odn recognition sequence.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of uncertainty in the discussion.

claim: HEGs are poised to be at the forefront of antagonistic coevolution between viruses and other MGEs.
source: Because of their selfish nature, ability to mobilize, nucleolytic activity, and enrichment within viral and mobile genomes, HEGs are poised to be at the forefront of antagonistic coevolution between viruses and other MGEs, and we anticipate that other putative HEGs have unrecognized antiparasite activities.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.
